segments.title: Graf Spee races back into the Atlantic
segments.summary: Graf Spee returns quickly to the Atlantic, where preparations for the next phase take precedence over immediate commerce raiding.
segments.body: Admiral Graf Spee is back in the Atlantic after Langsdorff avoided lingering in its other operating areas. The raider would still attack a suitable target if one appeared, but preparations for the next phase now took priority. The ship needed to make itself ready and harder to find before continuing the cruise. Speed, concealment, and logistics mattered as much to its survival as finding another merchant ship.

evidence.note: The transcript describes Graf Spee's rapid Atlantic return and says other preparations now take priority over hunting targets.

segments.title: Altmark provides supplies for Graf Spee's disguises
segments.summary: At the 24 November rendezvous, Altmark provides fuel and supplies used to fabricate disguises and prepare Graf Spee for the rest of its raiding cruise.
segments.body: The 24 November meeting with the supply ship Altmark involved more than routine refuelling. Stores carried by Altmark, together with supplies taken from captured merchant ships, gave Admiral Graf Spee material for disguises and other preparations. A later recap groups refuelling, disguise construction, and general preparation within the same rendezvous. Surface raiding depended on this mobile support and on captured stores, which helped the warship preserve its freedom of action.

evidence.note: The transcript dates the Altmark rendezvous to 24 November and connects its supplies to disguise construction and continued operations.
The recap explicitly describes Graf Spee as refuelling and building disguises.

segments.title: Altmark takes prisoners and perhaps more weapons
segments.summary: Graf Spee transfers more captured merchant seamen and officers to Altmark. Additional weapons may have passed between the ships during the same quiet rendezvous.
segments.body: Altmark receives more prisoners from Graf Spee, including captured merchant seamen and some officers. Another transfer of weapons may also have taken place during this comparatively calm meeting, although the exact date is uncertain. Some chronologies put it earlier or later. The 24 November rendezvous is presented as the likeliest occasion because the ships were under less pressure, so the prisoner movement is more securely dated than the possible weapons transfer.

evidence.note: The transcript describes prisoner transfers and explains the qualified dating of additional weapons transferred to Altmark.

segments.title: Forces H and K search behind Graf Spee
segments.summary: Royal Navy hunter groups sweep through Graf Spee's former cruising grounds, but their estimate of the raider's pace leaves them searching after Langsdorff has already escaped.
segments.body: Between 20 November and 2 December, Forces H and K move far south after passing through Graf Spee's former Atlantic cruising area, almost to the Indian Ocean. British planners expected the German ship to move more slowly and timed their interception around that estimate. Fuel and supplies gave the hunter groups about six days in the area to watch for the raider. Langsdorff had driven Graf Spee onward and escaped before the net closed. Their experience shows how endurance planning depends on a sound estimate of an enemy's operational tempo. Even a powerful hunter group cannot affect the chase if it searches in the wrong place at the wrong time.

evidence.note: The transcript maps Forces H and K southward, describes their six-day patrol endurance, and attributes the failed interception to an underestimate of Graf Spee's speed of movement.

segments.title: Forces H and K are absent from the River Plate battle
segments.summary: When the southern search ends, the hunter groups turn north and remain far from the 13 December Battle of the River Plate.
segments.body: After 2 December, the hunter groups turn north. The move leaves them far from South America when Graf Spee meets the British cruisers at the Battle of the River Plate on 13 December. Their failed southern search explains why Forces H and K were not close enough to join the later battle. Ships assigned to hunt the raider could not influence the engagement because they had been sent toward its earlier cruising area.

evidence.note: The transcript says the groups returned north and were consequently distant when the Battle of the River Plate occurred on 13 December.
